newsitem.title: GERMANY: Porsche net profit jumps in fiscal 1996.
newsitem.headline: Porsche net profit jumps in fiscal 1996.

text.p: Profits at Porsche AG came in even higher in fiscal 1996 than the company had forecast and will be at least 25 million marks ($17 million), a Porsche spokesman said Tuesday.

Porsche, which earned only 2.1 million marks ($1.4 million) in fiscal 1995, had previously said profits for the year ended July 31, 1996, would about double the net profit of 10.3 million marks ($7 million) posted in the first half.
The sports car maker's chairman, Wendelin Wiedeking, made the forecast last spring.
The improved results were due to the undying popularity of the company's 30-year old 911 model, the only car Porsche makes, company spokesman Anton Hunger said.
He said pretax profit for fiscal 1996 would "certainly at least reach 25 million marks."
Porsche previously said sales for the year ended on July 31 rose 7.7 percent to 2.8 billion marks ($1.9 billion) from 2.6 billion marks ($1.8 billion).
The company will present a detailed accounting of its results in December.
Sales growth has been strongest in the United States, but weak in Germany, where changes in tax law have hurt demand.
Porsche, which nearly went bankrupt in the early 1990s, had been led back to solid profits by Wiedeking, who sharply cut costs and eliminated some models.
Analysts expect Porsche earnings to continue climbing in the next few years.
The company will bring its long-awaited roadster model to market in October and dealers have already received orders for more than 13,000 of the vehicles, almost equal to one year's production.

Wiedeking said last month that the company was talking with its work force about expanding production beyond the stated capacity of around 30,000 units if demand for the 911 remains strong, according to a Porsche spokesman.
